procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Gujarat High Court dated October 23, 1969, dismissing in limine Criminal Revision No. 407 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Judicial Magistrate, Kaloi granted the railway administration's application under s. 138 of the Indian Railways Act on August 30, 1969.
2. Appellant's revision from the order of the Judicial Magistrate was dismissed by the Sessions Judge on October 4, 1969.
3. The appellant filed a criminal revision against the Sessions Judge's order in the Gujarat High Court, which was dismissed in limine by Shelat J. on October 23, 1969.
4. The appellant had also approached the Gujarat High Court by certiorari challenging the order of fine imposed on him, relying on the objection that the imposition of the fine was in violation of Art. 311 of the Constitution. This writ petition was rejected on August 25, 1969.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave challenging the order of the Gujarat High Court. The appellant appeared in person. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: This appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant, who was allotted railway stalls under a contract, could be classified as a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act.

facts: The appellant was allotted a tea stall and a refreshment stall at a railway station under two separate, identical agreements with the railway administration.
The agreements stipulated that the appellant was to run the stalls in accordance with the directions of the railway administration.
law: The definition of a 'railway servant' is found in section 3(7) read in conjunction with section 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act.
The Court approved of the reasoning in previous cases, specifically S. L. Puri v. Emperor and R. L. Mazumdar v. Alfred Ernest.
application: The Court examined the terms of the agreements governing the relationship between the appellant and the railway administration.
It found that the agreements expressly gave the railway administration "extensive power of directing and regulating the appellant's work and also of controlling the manner of doing the work."
This high degree of control exercised by the railway administration over the appellant's work was the key factor in the Court's decision.
Because the railway could direct and control the manner of his work, the appellant's status was deemed to be that of a 'railway servant' under the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim and held that he was a 'railway servant' because the terms of his contract gave the railway administration extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the manner in which he operated the stalls, thus fitting the definition under sections 3(7) and 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination of the appellant's contract amounted to a valid 'discharge' for the purpose of initiating proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.

facts: The appellant ran two stalls at a railway station under agreements with the railway administration.
The railway administration terminated these agreements.
When the appellant did not vacate the stalls, the railway administration initiated proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act to secure possession.
The appellant argued before the Sessions Court that even if he was a railway servant, the termination of his contract was not a valid 'discharge' as required by the Act.
law: Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act provides a summary remedy for the railway administration to recover property from a railway servant who has been 'discharged'.
application: The Sessions Judge considered the appellant's argument but disagreed with it.
The Judge held that the termination of the contract was equivalent to the appellant's 'discharge' for the purposes of the Act.
Based on this finding, the Sessions Judge concluded that proceedings under Section 138 could be lawfully initiated against the appellant.
The Magistrate also found that the appellant's service had been "lawfully discharged."
The High Court dismissed the appellant's revision petition, and the Supreme Court reviewed and upheld the conclusions of these lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument by sustaining the conclusions of the lower courts. It implicitly affirmed the view that the termination of the appellant's contract amounted to a valid 'discharge,' thereby satisfying the prerequisite for initiating summary repossession proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether proceedings for summary delivery of property under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act could be lawfully initiated against the appellant following the termination of his contract.

facts: The appellant operated a tea stall and a refreshment stall at a railway station under two agreements with the railway administration.
These agreements stipulated that the appellant had to run the stalls according to the directions of the railway administration.
The agreements were terminated by the railway administration after the appellant committed irregularities, was fined, and failed to pay the fine or vacate the premises upon notice.
Following the termination, the railway administration initiated proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act to secure summary possession of the stalls.
law: Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act provides a summary remedy for the delivery of railway property detained by a railway servant.
Section 3(7) read with Section 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act defines who qualifies as a 'railway servant'.
application: The Supreme Court first determined whether the appellant was a 'railway servant' under the Act.
It held that he was, because the terms of his agreements gave the railway administration extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the manner in which he did his work.
The Court found that the termination of the appellant's contracts amounted to his 'discharge' as a railway servant.

Since the appellant was a discharged railway servant who refused to deliver railway property (the stalls), the Court concluded that the conditions for initiating summary proceedings under Section 138 were met.

The Court also rejected the appellant's argument that he was entitled to the constitutional protection of Article 311, stating he was not a member of the civil service and his rights were governed solely by the terms of his agreements. His proper remedy for a potentially wrongful termination was a civil suit, not resisting the statutory eviction process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge, holding that proceedings for summary delivery of property under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act were lawfully initiated against him. This was because, due to the extensive control the railway had over his work under the agreements, he was deemed a 'railway servant', and the termination of his contract constituted a 'discharge', making him subject to this specific provision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of a master-servant relationship is a question of fact depending on the terms of the agreement as a whole.

facts: A dispute arose between a licensee running two stalls at a railway station and the railway administration.
The central question was whether the licensee qualified as a "railway servant" under the Indian Railways Act.
This determination was crucial because it dictated the legal process the railway could use to repossess the stalls after terminating the agreements.
law: The Supreme Court established that the relationship of master and servant is fundamentally characterized by an agreement of service, which can be either express or implied.
application: The Court ruled that determining whether a specific agreement creates a master-servant relationship is not a question of law, but a "question of fact."
This factual determination must be made by considering the terms of the agreement "as a whole."

In this specific case, the lower courts had examined the agreements and found that the railway administration reserved extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the licensee's work, leading them to conclude he was a railway servant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the principle that the existence of a master-servant relationship is a question of fact. It must be decided by examining the complete terms of the specific agreement between the parties to see if they constitute an agreement of service.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was any legal infirmity in the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge that would justify interference by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant's contracts to run tea and refreshment stalls were terminated by the railway administration.
The railway sought to repossess the stalls through a summary procedure under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.
The Magistrate, the Sessions Judge, and the High Court all ruled against the appellant, finding that he was a 'railway servant' for the purposes of the Act and could be dispossessed.
The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower court orders contained legal errors.
law: The Supreme Court's power to interfere with lower court orders under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and is exercised only when there is a 'legal infirmity' in the orders.
Article 311 of the Constitution provides certain protections to government servants against dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank.
The Indian Railways Act defines a 'railway servant' for the purposes of that specific Act, including for summary repossession of property under Section 138.
application: The Supreme Court examined the appellant's main argument: that because he was deemed a 'railway servant' under the Railways Act, he was automatically entitled to the constitutional protections of Article 311.

The Court dismissed this argument as 'wholly misconceived' and based on a 'misunderstanding' of Article 311, clarifying that being a 'railway servant' for the limited purpose of the Railways Act does not make one a civil servant entitled to Article 311 protection.
The Court also considered and rejected the appellant's allegation that the Magistrate's order was inspired by malice, finding no warrant for such an assumption.

The Court agreed with the reasoning of the lower courts that the appellant was indeed a 'railway servant' within the meaning of the Indian Railways Act, against whom action could be taken under Section 138.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it was unable to find any legal infirmity in the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge. Since the appellant's legal arguments were misconceived and no error was found in the lower courts' decisions, there was no justification for the Supreme Court to interfere under its special jurisdiction granted by Article 136 of the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant, who was allotted railway stalls under a contract, could be classified as a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant denied that he was a 'railway servant'.
respondent_arguments: The appellant was a 'railway servant' by virtue of Sections 3(7) and 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the termination of the appellant's contract amounted to a valid 'discharge' for the purpose of initiating proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that even if he was a railway servant, he had not been validly discharged.
respondent_arguments: The termination of the contract amounted to a valid 'discharge' of the appellant, allowing for proceedings under Section 138.

arguments.issue_text: Whether proceedings for summary delivery of property under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act could be lawfully initiated against the appellant following the termination of his contract.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that proceedings under Section 138 were unlawful because no notice to deliver possession of the stalls was given to him before the application was filed.
respondent_arguments: Proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act for summary delivery of property were lawfully initiated against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the determination of a master-servant relationship is a question of fact depending on the terms of the agreement as a whole.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the nature of the relationship should be determined by considering all facts, including the purpose of the allotment for his rehabilitation as a displaced person, and sought to introduce external evidence to prove this.
respondent_arguments: The nature of the relationship should be determined exclusively by the written agreements, which were conclusive on the matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was any legal infirmity in the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge that would justify interference by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that as a railway servant, he was entitled to the protection of Article 311 of the Constitution, and the denial of this protection constituted a legal infirmity in the lower courts' orders.
respondent_arguments: There was no legal infirmity in the orders of the lower courts, as the appellant's claim for protection under Article 311 was misconceived.

cases.principle: To support the conclusion that the appellant was a 'railway servant' as defined in s. 3(7) read with s. 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act, against whom action could be taken under s. 138, based on the terms of the agreements which gave the Railway administration extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the work.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional protection under Article 311 is only afforded to a member of a civil service who has been dismissed, removed, or reduced in rank. The determination of whether a master-servant relationship exists is a question of fact dependent on the terms of the service agreement as a whole.
obiter: If a person's rights are confined to a written agreement and they believe the agreement has been wrongfully terminated, they may challenge such termination in the civil courts to seek available legal relief.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The terms which govern the parties expressly reserve to the railway administration extensive power of directing and regulating the appellant's work and also, to an extent, of controlling the manner of doing the work. The retention of this power by the railway administration, in our view, constitutes relevant material for sustaining the conclusion of the courts below that the appellant is a railway servant, as defined in s. 3(7) read with s. 148(2). legal_tests_applied: The relationship of master and servant is characterised by agreement of service, express or implied, and whether or not a given agreement is one of service is a question of fact depending on its terms considered as a whole.
To claim the benefit of Article 311 of the Constitution, a person must be a member of the civil service and must have been dismissed, removed or reduced in rank.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's claim for protection under Article 311 of the Constitution was rejected because: 'The appellant is neither a member of the civil service as coJJtemplated by this Article nor has he been dismissed, removed or reduced in rank so as to attract the pro-tection of sub-Art ( 2) of this Article.'

The appellant's rights were strictly limited by his contract, and his proper remedy for alleged wrongful termination was in the civil courts, not by challenging the summary proceedings. The court stated: 'The appellant's rights are clearly confinea to the written agreements and if he feels aggrieved by anything done by the railway administration which he considers to be in breach of the terms -of the agreements, he is at full liberty to seek redress in accordance with law in the ordinary civil courts.'

The Supreme Court found no reason to intervene with the lower courts' decisions, stating: 'So far as the impugned order of the High Court and the order of the Sessions Judge is concerned we are unable to find any legal infirmity which would justify interference by this Court under Art. 136 of the Constitution.'
why_respondent_won: The railway administration was found to have a master-servant relationship with the appellant because the agreements reserved to it 'extensive power of directing and regulating the appellant's work and also, to an extent, of controlling the manner of doing the work.'

This master-servant relationship established the appellant as a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act, which lawfully permitted the railway to initiate summary proceedings for delivery of property under Section 138 of the Act.
policy_considerations: Keeping in view the purpose and object of these agreements, namely, that of affording necessary amenities to the travelling public, retention of this over• all power by the railway administration is not only appropriate but necessary.
